lessons.title: History of cryptography: from the scytale to Enigma
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a stick wrapped in a leather strip covered with letters, next to a cipher disk with two rings of letters.
objectives: Tell apart substitution, transposition, code and steganography.
Explain why frequency analysis breaks monoalphabetic ciphers.
Describe the one-time pad and the conditions for its perfect secrecy.
Place the major milestones up to modern cryptography (DES, Diffie-Hellman, RSA, AES).

references.title: C. E. Shannon, "Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems", Bell System Technical Journal, 1949

blocks.text: Why history matters in the exam

Ancient ciphers are broken in seconds today, but they show the two basic operations found in modern algorithms: replacing symbols (substitution) and moving them (transposition). AES still combines these two ideas, on a large scale and with a secret key.
The basic operations

blocks.title: Substitution cipher (chiffre par substitution)
blocks.text: Each letter is replaced by another letter or a symbol. The Caesar cipher shifts each letter three places in the alphabet: A becomes D, B becomes E.

blocks.title: Transposition cipher (chiffre par transposition)
blocks.text: The letters stay the same but change place. The Spartan scytale is the typical example: a strip wrapped around a stick can only be read with a stick of the same diameter.

blocks.title: Steganography (stéganographie)
blocks.text: Hiding the very existence of the message (invisible ink, data slipped into the pixels of an image) instead of making it unreadable. It is often combined with encryption.

rows: A letter always gives the same encrypted letter
The same letter changes according to its position and the key
Whole words replaced using a codebook
Nothing is encrypted: the message is hidden

blocks.text: The first cryptanalysis: counting letters

In a language, some letters come up more often than others: E in French as in English. With a monoalphabetic cipher, the most frequent letter of the encrypted message therefore probably stands for E. The Arab scholar Al-Kindi described this frequency analysis in the 9th century: it is the first known method of cryptanalysis.

blocks.title: From the scytale to AES
blocks.alt: Six-step timeline: the scytale of Antiquity (transposition); the Caesar cipher in the 1st century BC (shift); the Vigenère cipher in the 16th century (several alphabets); the Enigma machine during the Second World War (rotors); the modern era with DES in 1977, Diffie-Hellman in 1976 and RSA in 1977; AES adopted in 2001.

blocks.text: Vigenère and Enigma: several alphabets

The Vigenère cipher (16th century) uses a keyword: each letter of the message is shifted by a value that depends on the matching letter of the key. The same plaintext letter therefore gives different encrypted letters, which blurs frequency analysis. Its weakness: the key repeats. In 1863, Friedrich Kasiski published a method to find the key length from the repetitions; each position is then broken like a Caesar cipher.

The Enigma machine, used by the German army during the Second World War, automates a polyalphabetic substitution: rotors turn with each keystroke. Polish mathematicians, with Marian Rejewski from 1932, then the Bletchley Park team, including Alan Turing, broke it by relying on procedural errors and predictable messages.

blocks.title: The lesson of Enigma
blocks.text: The machine was solid on paper; it was the procedures (badly chosen keys, phrases repeated every day) that gave it away. Even today, most failures come from implementation and key management, not from the algorithm.
The one-time pad and perfect secrecy

blocks.title: One-time pad (masque jetable)
blocks.text: Vernam cipher (1917): the message is combined with a random key of the same length, for example with an exclusive OR. Claude Shannon proved in 1949 that it is unbreakable if the key is truly random, as long as the message, kept secret and used only once.

blocks.title: The limits of the one-time pad
items: Reusing the key for a second message makes it possible to combine the two encrypted messages and recover the plaintexts.
Secretly distributing a key as long as all the messages is very difficult: the one-time pad remains reserved for rare uses.

blocks.title: Kerckhoffs's principle (principe de Kerckhoffs)
blocks.text: Stated in 1883: the security of an encryption system must rest on the secrecy of the key, not on that of the algorithm. A public, well-studied algorithm inspires more confidence than a "secret" algorithm.

In the exam, remember three pairs: substitution (replace) and transposition (move); monoalphabetic (a single alphabet) and polyalphabetic (several); encryption (make unreadable) and steganography (hide). The one-time pad is the only cipher proven unbreakable, under four conditions.

blocks.title: SOC case: a home-made "encryption" in the lab
blocks.text: Simulated exercise in the training lab: a fictitious internal script "protects" passwords by shifting each character three places. The analyst notices that the character frequency looks like that of a plaintext: it is a Caesar cipher, not a protection. The analyst recommends a slow hash function for passwords and a standard algorithm such as AES for data, then opens a ticket for the development team.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: a home-made or "secret" algorithm is a warning sign, in line with Kerckhoffs's principle.
SOC manager: an encoding (Base64) or a simple shift protects nothing; the analyst must be able to recognize them.
Auditor: asks which standard algorithms are used and how the keys are managed.
Risk manager: the great historical failures came from procedures; so key management is assessed too.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Caesar and Atbash are monoalphabetic substitutions; the scytale is a transposition.
Vigenère is polyalphabetic: you must first find the key length before frequency analysis.
Steganography hides the existence of the message; it does not encrypt it.
The one-time pad is only perfect if the key is random, as long as the message, secret and never reused.
An encoding such as Base64 is not encryption: there is no key.
Substitution: replace; transposition: move.
Monoalphabetic: broken by frequency analysis (Al-Kindi, 9th century).
Polyalphabetic (Vigenère, Enigma): stronger, broken thanks to key repetition and procedural errors.
One-time pad: perfect secrecy proven by Shannon, under strict conditions.
Kerckhoffs: only the secrecy of the key counts.
Modern era: Diffie-Hellman 1976, DES and RSA 1977, AES 2001.

lessons.title: Quantum and post-quantum cryptography
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a stylized atom next to an open padlock, then a reinforced closed padlock, linked by an arrow.
objectives: Explain what a quantum computer would change (Shor's and Grover's algorithms).
Tell apart post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution.
Name the NIST FIPS 203, 204 and 205 standards and their use.
Prepare a migration: inventory, priorities, agility, hybridization.

references.title: NIST FIPS 203, Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM), 2024
NIST FIPS 204, Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA), 2024
NIST FIPS 205, Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA), 2024
NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards

blocks.text: What changes with the quantum computer

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer would run algorithms that are impossible to carry out at scale today. Such a machine does not yet exist at the necessary size, but two mathematical results already show what it would break and what it would weaken.

rows: Broken: factoring and discrete logarithm become easy
Accelerated search: security in bits is roughly halved

blocks.title: Harvest now, decrypt later (récolter maintenant, déchiffrer plus tard)
blocks.text: An attacker records encrypted exchanges today in order to decrypt them the day a quantum computer becomes available. Data that must stay secret for a long time is therefore already exposed.
Two answers not to confuse

blocks.title: Post-quantum cryptography, PQC (cryptographie post-quantique)
blocks.text: New classical algorithms, run on our current computers, based on problems thought to be hard even for a quantum computer: lattices, hash functions…

blocks.title: Quantum key distribution, QKD (distribution quantique de clés)
blocks.text: Key exchange that uses photons: any eavesdropping disturbs the signal and is detected. Reference protocol: BB84 (Bennett and Brassard, 1984). It requires dedicated hardware, a limited distance and an already authenticated channel. This is what is called "quantum cryptography".
The 2024 NIST standards

These three standards were approved by NIST in August 2024. ML-KEM and ML-DSA rely on lattices; SLH-DSA relies only on hash functions, a very well-studied basis, at the cost of larger signatures. Others are following: FN-DSA, derived from Falcon, and HQC, selected in 2025 as a second encapsulation mechanism.
Preparing the migration

blocks.title: Migrating to post-quantum
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: inventory the uses of RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman; prioritize according to the lifetime of the data; make systems agile so the algorithm can be changed by configuration; first deploy hybrid classical and post-quantum modes; test then switch over.

blocks.title: The right reflexes
items: Inventory where RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman are used: certificates, TLS, VPN, code signing.
Classify data by how long it must stay secret: the longest first.
Require crypto agility: change the algorithm by configuration, without rewriting the application.
Use hybrid modes (classical and post-quantum) during the transition, as recommended by ANSSI and BSI.
Move symmetric encryption to AES-256 and hashes to SHA-384 or more where possible.

blocks.title: A timetable taking shape
blocks.text: In the United States, the target set for the federal administration is to have completed the migration by 2035, with earlier deadlines for the most sensitive systems. The NIST IR 8547 report supports this transition. Check the current version before quoting a precise date.
The classic trap: "quantum cryptography" (QKD, photons) is not "post-quantum cryptography" (new algorithms on classical computers). Another reflex: Shor breaks asymmetric, Grover weakens symmetric.

blocks.title: SOC case: the lab's cryptographic inventory
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: the training lab SOC helps prepare the migration. From the TLS logs and the certificate inventory of a fictitious environment, it lists the RSA and ECDHE key exchanges, the VPNs and the code signatures. Flows that carry data to be kept secret for ten years (simulated HR files) come first. The SOC also adds a rule that flags downgrades to obsolete suites.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: the post-quantum migration is a multi-year program: inventory, budget, requirements for suppliers.
SOC manager: TLS logs and the certificate inventory give the map of uses.
Auditor: checks that an inventory exists and that contracts require crypto agility.
Risk manager: prioritizes according to the lifetime of the data, not according to a supposed arrival date of the quantum computer.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: QKD (photons) is not PQC (classical algorithms).
Shor targets asymmetric cryptography (RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman); Grover targets symmetric cryptography and hashing, with security in bits roughly halved.
AES-256 is still considered solid: it is not "broken" by quantum computing.
ML-KEM is used to establish a key; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are used to sign.
The risk already exists for long-lived data: harvest now, decrypt later.
Shor breaks RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman; Grover roughly halves the security of symmetric cryptography.
Harvest now, decrypt later: lasting secrets are already exposed.
PQC: new algorithms on classical computers; QKD: key exchange using photons.
NIST 2024: FIPS 203 ML-KEM (keys), FIPS 204 ML-DSA and FIPS 205 SLH-DSA (signatures).
Migration: inventory, priorities, agility, hybrid, tests.

lessons.title: Advances in cryptography
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three cubes linked by chain links, each bearing a small fingerprint, next to a closed box from which a result comes out.
objectives: Explain what homomorphic encryption, multi-party computation and zero-knowledge proofs are for.
Describe what a blockchain provides and what it does not.
Name lightweight cryptography, format-preserving encryption and authenticated encryption.
Choose the technique suited to a given need.

references.title: NIST SP 800-38G, Methods for Format-Preserving Encryption
NIST SP 800-232 (2025), Ascon-Based Lightweight Cryptography Standards for Constrained Devices

blocks.text: Protecting data in its three states

We have long known how to protect stored data (disk encryption) or transmitted data (TLS, IPsec). The recent challenge is to protect it while it is being used: new techniques make it possible to compute without seeing the data.

blocks.title: The three states of data
blocks.alt: Three-step diagram: at rest, protected by disk or database encryption (AES); in transit, protected by TLS or IPsec; in use, protected by homomorphic encryption, multi-party computation or hardware enclaves.

blocks.text: Computing without seeing the data

blocks.title: Homomorphic encryption (chiffrement homomorphe)
blocks.text: Makes it possible to compute on encrypted data: once decrypted, the result is the same as if the computation had been done on the plaintext. The first fully homomorphic scheme was published in 2009 by Craig Gentry. It remains much slower than a classical computation.

blocks.title: Secure multi-party computation, MPC (calcul multipartite sécurisé)
blocks.text: Several parties jointly compute a result (an average, a comparison, the elements common to two lists) without revealing their data to the others.

blocks.title: Zero-knowledge proof, ZKP (preuve à divulgation nulle de connaissance)
blocks.text: Proving that a statement is true, or that you know a secret, without revealing the secret itself. Example: proving you are of age without giving your date of birth.

blocks.title: Confidential computing (informatique confidentielle)
blocks.text: Protecting data during processing thanks to hardware enclaves, called trusted execution environments: even the machine's administrator cannot see the data being processed.
Blockchains

blocks.title: Blockchain (chaîne de blocs)
blocks.text: Shared ledger in which each block contains the hash of the previous block. Modifying an old block would change all the following hashes: tampering shows. Bitcoin, described in 2008, is its first major use.

rows: Confidentiality: by default, everything is readable
The accuracy of the data entered in the first place
Timestamping that is hard to dispute

blocks.text: Other techniques to know

rows: Connected objects, sensors, very low-power cards
Encrypt a number while keeping its format (16 digits)
Confidentiality and integrity in a single operation

blocks.title: Sticking to standards
blocks.text: These techniques are promising, but Kerckhoffs's principle still holds: choose proven libraries and standardized algorithms, never a home-made construction.
"Rest, transit, use: AES for the disk, TLS for the network, homomorphic encryption and enclaves for computation."

blocks.title: SOC case: sharing indicators without exposing your customers
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: two fictitious SOCs want to know whether they have seen the same malicious IP addresses, without revealing the full list of their customers. The trainer presents a multi-party computation approach (private set intersection): each one learns only the common addresses. The exercise uses only made-up data.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: these techniques open up new uses (cloud, data sharing) but cost performance; they are reserved for the cases that justify them.
SOC manager: a blockchain does not replace a protected log; write-once storage and hashes are often enough to prove log integrity.
Auditor: asks which standard the solution relies on and who audited its implementation.
Risk manager: on a public blockchain, a mistake or a leak is irreversible; the risk of losing private keys is assessed too.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Homomorphic: computation on encrypted data; it is not hashing.
ZKP: you prove without revealing the secret.
Blockchain: integrity and traceability, not confidentiality.
FPE keeps the format of the data; it changes nothing about the key length.
Lightweight cryptography: for constrained devices, not to speed up a server.
Data at rest, in transit, in use: each state has its protections.
Homomorphic: compute on encrypted data; MPC: compute together without revealing; ZKP: prove without revealing.
Confidential computing: hardware enclaves during processing.
Blockchain: chained hashes, integrity and traceability, no confidentiality.
Lightweight cryptography (Ascon), FPE (SP 800-38G), AEAD (AES-GCM).

questions.prompt: The Spartan scytale, a strip wound around a rod, uses which method?
questions.explanation: The letters stay the same; only their order changes when the strip is unwound: this is a transposition.

whyNot.0: A substitution replaces the letters; the scytale keeps them.
whyNot.1: The strip is visible: the message is not hidden, only unreadable.
whyNot.2: Several substitution alphabets: that is Vigenère or Enigma.

questions.prompt: Which technique broke monoalphabetic ciphers such as Caesar's?
questions.explanation: The same letter always gives the same ciphertext letter: the frequencies of the language remain visible (a method described by Al-Kindi).

whyNot.1: It forces a protocol to use a weak version.
whyNot.2: It targets collisions in hash functions.
whyNot.3: It measures the timing or power consumption of a device.

questions.prompt: Why does the Vigenère cipher resist frequency analysis better than Caesar?
choices: It moves the letters without replacing them
The same letter can give several different letters
Its key is as long as the message
It hides the very existence of the message
questions.explanation: The shift depends on the letter of the key: the same plaintext letter gives different ciphertext letters.

whyNot.0: It is a substitution, not a transposition.
whyNot.2: Its key repeats; it is the one-time pad that uses a key as long as the message.
whyNot.3: That is the definition of steganography.

questions.prompt: Which TWO conditions are necessary for the perfect security of the one-time pad?
choices: A key shorter than the message
questions.explanation: Shannon: a random key, as long as the message, secret and never reused.

whyNot.1: On the contrary, the key must be at least as long as the message.
whyNot.3: The algorithm (an exclusive OR) can be public: this is Kerckhoffs's principle.

questions.prompt: What does Kerckhoffs's principle state?
choices: Security relies on the secrecy of the algorithm
Security relies on the secrecy of the key
Each message requires a new algorithm
The key must be as long as the message
questions.explanation: A public, thoroughly studied algorithm is safer; only the secrecy of the key should protect the data.

whyNot.0: That is the opposite of the principle: "security through obscurity".
whyNot.2: That is neither realistic nor required.
whyNot.3: That is a condition of the one-time pad.

questions.prompt: What mainly made it possible to break Enigma during the war?
choices: A simple frequency analysis of the letters
A single key valid for the whole war
questions.explanation: Polish and then British cryptanalysts exploited repeated phrases and mistakes in how keys were used.

whyNot.0: Enigma is polyalphabetic: letter frequencies are scrambled.
whyNot.2: The rotors turned with every keystroke: the alphabet kept changing.

questions.prompt: An image contains a message hidden in its pixels, with no encryption at all. What is this?
questions.explanation: The message is not made unreadable: its existence is concealed.

whyNot.0: A code replaces words using a codebook.
whyNot.1: A hash produces a digest; it does not hide a message.
whyNot.3: A transposition moves the letters of a visible message.

questions.prompt: Which quantum algorithm threatens RSA and elliptic curves?
questions.explanation: Shor efficiently solves factoring and the discrete logarithm, on which RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman rely.

whyNot.0: Grover speeds up searching: it weakens symmetric encryption without breaking it.
whyNot.1: BB84 is a quantum key distribution protocol.
whyNot.3: Rijndael is the algorithm that became AES.

questions.prompt: What is the expected effect of Grover's algorithm on AES-256?
questions.explanation: Grover roughly halves the security in bits: AES-256 keeps about 128 bits, which remains strong.

whyNot.2: Grover does speed up the key search.
whyNot.3: That would be the effect on a 128-bit key.

questions.prompt: What is post-quantum cryptography?
choices: A key exchange based on photons
Encryption run on a quantum computer
questions.explanation: These are classical algorithms, based on problems believed to be hard even for a quantum computer.

whyNot.2: A larger RSA key does not resist Shor.

questions.prompt: Which 2024 NIST standard is used to establish a shared key?
questions.explanation: ML-KEM is a key encapsulation mechanism derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber.

whyNot.1: AES encrypts data with a key that is already shared.

questions.prompt: Why is data encrypted with RSA today already at risk?
choices: RSA is already broken by today's computers
Grover directly recovers the RSA private key
It can be stored now and decrypted later
questions.explanation: An attacker can record the exchanges today and wait for a quantum computer able to run Shor.

whyNot.0: The lifetime of a certificate does not depend on quantum computing.
whyNot.1: No current computer breaks RSA with a proper key size.
whyNot.2: It is Shor, not Grover, that threatens RSA.

questions.prompt: What is the FIRST step of a post-quantum migration?
choices: Replace all certificates in one go
Move all RSA keys to 8192 bits
Inventory the uses of asymmetric cryptography
questions.explanation: Without an inventory of where RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman are used, you can neither prioritize nor plan.

whyNot.0: A sudden switch breaks compatibility; hybrid modes are used along the way.
whyNot.1: A longer RSA key does not resist Shor.
whyNot.3: QKD requires dedicated hardware and does not replace signatures.

questions.prompt: What does quantum key distribution (QKD) make possible?
choices: Encrypting large volumes without any key
Doing without an already authenticated channel
Detecting eavesdropping during the key exchange
Signing documents in a post-quantum way
questions.explanation: Any measurement of the photons by an eavesdropper disturbs the signal: eavesdropping can be detected (BB84 protocol).

whyNot.0: It provides a key, which is then used to encrypt.
whyNot.1: On the contrary, it requires an authenticated channel.
whyNot.3: It exchanges keys; it does not sign.

questions.prompt: Which technique makes it possible to compute on data that stays encrypted?
questions.explanation: The decrypted result is the same as if the computation had been done on the plaintext data.

whyNot.0: A hash cannot be decrypted and is not used for computing.
whyNot.1: It hides a message; it does not compute.
whyNot.3: It keeps the format of the data but does not allow computing on it.

questions.prompt: A user proves they are of legal age without revealing their date of birth. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: A zero-knowledge proof establishes that a statement is true without revealing the secret.

whyNot.0: It encrypts the date; the verifier could conclude nothing without the key.

questions.prompt: What does a blockchain mainly provide?
choices: The confidentiality of all the data
The accuracy of the data entered at the start
The protection of the members' private keys
The integrity and traceability of the records
questions.explanation: Each block contains the hash of the previous one: any modification shows.

whyNot.0: By default, the records can be read by the participants.
whyNot.1: Data that is wrong at the start stays wrong, but well traced.
whyNot.2: Everyone remains responsible for their own private keys.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to encrypt card numbers while keeping 16 digits. Which technique?
questions.explanation: FPE (NIST SP 800-38G) produces an encrypted result that keeps the original format.

whyNot.0: It proves a statement; it does not encrypt a number.
whyNot.1: It is used to compute on encrypted data; it does not keep the format.

questions.prompt: Two SOCs want their shared indicators without revealing the rest of their lists. Which technique?
questions.explanation: With private set intersection, each party learns only the common elements.

whyNot.1: Encrypting while keeping the format does not allow comparing without revealing.
whyNot.2: Hiding the exchanges does not limit what the other party learns.
whyNot.3: Everything there would be readable by the participants.

questions.prompt: Which technique protects data while it is being processed, thanks to the hardware?
choices: The TLS 1.3 protocol between two servers
The digital signature of the code being run
questions.explanation: An enclave isolates the processing: even the machine's administrator cannot see the data.

whyNot.3: It proves the origin of the code, not the confidentiality of the data processed.

questions.prompt: Which choice best suits a very low-power industrial sensor?
choices: A lightweight algorithm such as Ascon
questions.explanation: Lightweight cryptography is designed for constrained devices; NIST selected Ascon.

whyNot.1: It requires an enormous amount of computation.
whyNot.2: Too costly in computation and energy for a small sensor.
whyNot.3: It has been broken since the 19th century.
